blocks.text: Q1. What is the difference between == and equals()?

== compares references (are both variables pointing to the same object in memory?). For primitives it compares values. equals() compares logical equality. The default implementation in Object is just this == obj, so you must override it to compare by field values.
Q2. What is the equals() contract?
An overridden equals() must be:
• Reflexive: x.equals(x) is true.
• Symmetric: if x.equals(y) then y.equals(x).
• Transitive: if x equals y and y equals z, then x equals z.
• Consistent: repeated calls return the same result if nothing used in the comparison changed.
• Non-null: x.equals(null) is always false (never throws).
Q3. What is the hashCode() contract?
• If two objects are equal per equals(), they must return the same hashCode.
• If two objects have the same hashCode, they are not necessarily equal (that is a collision).
• hashCode must return the same value on repeated calls during one execution, as long as the fields used in equals() do not change.
Rule of thumb: always override both together, using the same set of fields.

Q5. Why use getClass() instead of instanceof in equals()?

getClass() guarantees symmetry when subclasses add fields: a Manager will never equal an Employee. instanceof allows subclass instances to be equal to parent instances, which can break symmetry. Use instanceof when the class is final or when you deliberately want subclasses to compare equal (e.g. List implementations, where an ArrayList can equal a LinkedList with the same elements).
Q6. How does HashMap use hashCode() and equals() together?

On put/get, HashMap (1) calls hashCode() on the key, (2) spreads the bits and picks a bucket index, then (3) walks that bucket calling equals() to find the exact key. hashCode narrows the search to one bucket; equals picks the right entry within it.
Q7. What does Java 16+ record give you here?
A record automatically generates equals(), hashCode() and toString() based on all components, and its fields are final. That makes records ideal HashMap keys: record Point(int x, int y) {}.
Q8. What happens if you override equals() but not hashCode()?
Two logically equal objects get different identity hash codes, land in different buckets, and hash-based collections stop working: lookups fail and HashSet allows duplicates.

Q9. What happens if a key's fields change after it is put into a HashMap?

The entry stays in the bucket chosen from the old hashCode. Looking it up with the mutated key computes a new hash (wrong bucket); looking it up with an equal-to-original key finds the bucket but equals() fails. The entry is effectively lost (a memory leak). Keys should be immutable - this is why String and Integer make good keys.

Q10. What if hashCode() always returns a constant, e.g. 42?

It is legal (equal objects still have equal hashes) but terrible for performance: every entry lands in one bucket, so get/put degrade from O(1) to O(n). Since Java 8, HashMap converts a bucket into a red-black tree once it holds 8+ entries (and the table has at least 64 buckets), limiting the worst case to O(log n) - but only if keys are Comparable.
Q11. Give two Strings with the same hashCode.

Q12. Can you use an array as a HashMap key?

Technically yes, but arrays inherit identity-based equals/hashCode from Object, so new int[]{1,2} will never match another array with the same contents. Wrap it in a List or use a record, or compare with Arrays.equals() / Arrays.hashCode().

Q14. Why does remove() set data[--size] = null?
Without it, the array still holds a reference to the removed object, preventing garbage collection (a loitering reference / memory leak).
Q15. Why is the default growth 1.5x and not 2x?
It balances memory waste against the number of copy operations. Amortized add() is still O(1). oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1) is a cheap way to compute 1.5x.
Q16. What is a fail-fast iterator? How does it work?

It throws ConcurrentModificationException if the collection is structurally modified after the iterator is created (other than through iterator.remove()). The iterator saves expectedModCount and compares it to the list's modCount on each next(). Fail-safe iterators (e.g. CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap) iterate over a snapshot or tolerate concurrent changes instead.

Q19. Explain the internal working of HashMap and implement a simple version.
• An array of buckets (table), default capacity 16, always a power of two.
• Hash spreading: h ^ (h >>> 16) mixes high bits into low bits so they influence the bucket index.
• Index: hash & (n - 1), equivalent to modulo when n is a power of two, but faster.
• Collisions: entries in the same bucket form a linked list (treeified at 8+ since Java 8).
• Load factor 0.75: when size exceeds capacity x 0.75 the table doubles and entries are rehashed.
• One null key is allowed; it always goes to bucket 0.

Q28. Can two unequal objects have the same hashCode?
Yes - that's a collision. The contract only requires equal objects to share a hash.
Q29. Can two equal objects have different hashCodes?
No. That violates the contract and breaks every hash-based collection.
Q30. What is the default hashCode() of Object?
An identity hash code generated by the JVM (not the memory address in modern JVMs), stored in the object header once computed.
Q31. Why is String a good HashMap key?
It is immutable, final, and caches its hashCode after the first computation.
Q32. What is the time complexity of HashMap.get()?
O(1) average; worst case O(n) with a linked-list bucket, or O(log n) once the bucket is treeified (Java 8+).
Q33. What is the load factor and why 0.75?
The fill ratio that triggers resizing. 0.75 is a trade-off between memory use and collision probability.
Q34. What happens when two keys collide in Java 8+?
They are chained in the same bucket. If a bucket reaches 8 nodes and the table capacity is at least 64, it is converted to a red-black tree; it reverts to a list at 6.
Q35. How do you make a collection read-only?
Collections.unmodifiableList(list) (a view), or List.of(...) / List.copyOf(...) (truly immutable, no nulls).
Q36. How do you make a collection thread-safe?
Collections.synchronizedList/Map, or better, concurrent classes: ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentLinkedQueue.
Q37. Why does ConcurrentHashMap reject null keys and values?
In a concurrent setting, get() returning null would be ambiguous (absent vs mapped to null) and can't be safely disambiguated with containsKey().
Q38. What is IdentityHashMap?
A map that compares keys with == and System.identityHashCode() instead of equals()/hashCode().
Q39. What is WeakHashMap?
A map whose keys are held by weak references; entries are removed once the key is no longer strongly reachable. Useful for caches/metadata.
Q40. Difference between Iterator and ListIterator?
ListIterator works only on Lists, moves both directions, and supports add() and set() as well as remove().
Q41. Why should you not modify a list in a for-each loop?
for-each uses an Iterator; structural changes outside iterator.remove() trigger ConcurrentModificationException. Use iterator.remove() or removeIf().
Q42. Arrays.asList() vs List.of()?
Arrays.asList is fixed-size but allows set() and nulls, and writes through to the array. List.of is fully immutable and rejects nulls.
Q43. How does Lombok / IDE generate hashCode?
Typically 31 * result + field.hashCode() for each field. 31 is an odd prime, and 31 * i can be optimized to (i << 5) - i.

Questions 1 - 15
Q1. What are the main features introduced in Java 8?
Java 8 (released March 2014) was the biggest update to the language since generics. Its key features are:
• Lambda expressions - pass behaviour as data.
• Functional interfaces and the java.util.function package.
• Method references (Class::method).
• Default and static methods in interfaces.
• Stream API for declarative, pipeline-style processing of collections.
• Optional to model "maybe absent" values.
• New Date/Time API (java.time).
• CompletableFuture, StringJoiner, new Map methods, Base64, Nashorn JS engine, and Metaspace replacing PermGen.
Q2. What is a lambda expression?

A lambda expression is an anonymous function: a block of code with parameters and a body but no name, that can be passed around like a value. It provides the implementation of the single abstract method of a functional interface, which lets you write functional-style code with much less boilerplate than an anonymous inner class.
Q3. What are the different syntax forms of a lambda expression?
A lambda has three parts: a parameter list, the arrow ->, and a body. Parentheses, types, braces and
return are optional in many cases.
Rule: If the body is a single expression, its value is returned automatically. A block body { } needs an explicit return if it returns a value.
Q4. What is a functional interface?

A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM - Single Abstract Method). It may also contain any number of default methods, static methods, and abstract methods that override public methods of java.lang.Object (such as equals). Lambdas and method references can only be assigned to functional interface types.
Examples in the JDK: Runnable, Callable, Comparator, Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier.
Q5. What is the purpose of the @FunctionalInterface annotation? Is it mandatory?

@FunctionalInterface asks the compiler to check that the interface has exactly one abstract method. If someone adds a second abstract method, compilation fails. It is not mandatory - any interface with one abstract method is functional and works with lambdas - but it documents intent and protects against accidental changes.
Q6. Can a functional interface have default methods, static methods, or methods from Object?
Yes. Only abstract methods are counted. Default and static methods have bodies, so they do not count. Abstract methods that re-declare public Object methods (like boolean equals(Object o) in
Comparator) also do not count, because every implementation inherits them from Object anyway.
Q7. What is the difference between a lambda expression and an anonymous inner class?
• Class file: An anonymous class compiles to a separate .class file (e.g. Outer$1.class). A lambda does not; it is linked at runtime using invokedynamic.
• this keyword: Inside an anonymous class, this refers to the anonymous class instance. Inside a lambda, this refers to the enclosing class instance.
• Scope: An anonymous class creates a new scope, so it can shadow variables of the enclosing method. A lambda shares the enclosing scope and cannot redeclare a local variable with the same name.
• Target: An anonymous class can implement an interface with many abstract methods or extend an abstract/concrete class. A lambda can only implement a functional interface.
• State: An anonymous class can have its own fields; a lambda cannot.
Q8. What does "effectively final" mean? Why must captured variables be effectively final?
A local variable is effectively final if it is never reassigned after initialisation, even if it is not declared
final. Lambdas (and, since Java 8, anonymous classes) can only capture local variables that are final or effectively final.

The reason: a lambda captures a copy of the value, and it may run later or on another thread. Allowing the variable to change would cause confusing results and race conditions. Instance and static fields are not restricted, since they are accessed through a reference rather than copied.
Q9. What is target typing (type inference) in lambdas?
A lambda has no type of its own. The compiler infers its type from the context it is used in - the "target type". The same lambda can therefore become different functional interfaces:

Callable<String> c = () -> "done";   // target type Callable<String>
Supplier<String> s = () -> "done";   // target type Supplier<String>
Parameter types are also inferred from the target, which is why (a, b) -> a + b works without declaring int.
Q10. Can a lambda expression throw a checked exception?
Only if the functional interface's abstract method declares that exception. For example,
Callable.call() declares throws Exception, so a Callable lambda may throw checked exceptions, but
Function.apply() does not, so a Function lambda must catch them.
A common pattern is to define your own functional interface that declares throws Exception, or to wrap checked exceptions into unchecked ones.
Q11. What does "this" refer to inside a lambda?
this inside a lambda refers to the instance of the enclosing class, exactly as it would in the surrounding method. Lambdas are lexically scoped and do not introduce a new level of scope.
Q12. How are lambda expressions implemented internally?

The compiler does not generate an inner class. It moves the lambda body into a private synthetic method (such as lambda$main$0) and emits an invokedynamic instruction at the point where the lambda is created. The first time it runs, the JVM calls the LambdaMetafactory bootstrap method, which generates a lightweight class implementing the functional interface. Later calls reuse that linkage. Non-capturing lambdas are typically created once and cached. This approach makes startup cheaper and leaves the JVM free to improve the strategy later.
Q13. How do you sort a list using a lambda and Comparator?
Java 8 added Comparator.comparing, thenComparing, reversed, nullsFirst and nullsLast, which make multi-field sorting short and readable.

Q15. What are the advantages and limitations of lambda expressions?

Advantages: less boilerplate code; behaviour can be passed as a parameter; they enable the Stream API and functional style; collections can be processed in parallel easily; code is more readable for small operations.

Limitations: they work only with functional interfaces; they can capture only effectively final locals; checked exceptions are awkward to handle; stack traces are harder to read; long multi-line lambdas hurt readability (extract a method instead); they cannot hold state.
Questions 16 - 27
Q16. What does the java.util.function package contain?
It contains about 43 general-purpose functional interfaces so you rarely need to write your own. The four core ones are:
• Predicate<T> - boolean test(T t) - checks a condition.
• Function<T,R> - R apply(T t) - transforms a T into an R.
• Consumer<T> - void accept(T t) - takes a value, returns nothing.
• Supplier<T> - T get() - takes nothing, returns a value.

The rest are variations: two-argument versions (BiFunction, BiPredicate, BiConsumer), operators (UnaryOperator, BinaryOperator), and primitive versions (IntPredicate, ToIntFunction, IntSupplier and so on).
Q17. Explain Predicate with an example.
Predicate<T> represents a boolean-valued condition on one argument. Its abstract method is test(T
t). It is used by filter() in streams and by removeIf() on collections.
Q18. Explain Function with an example.
Function<T, R> takes an argument of type T and returns a result of type R through apply(T t). It is used by map() in streams.
Q19. Explain Consumer with an example.
Consumer<T> accepts a single argument and returns nothing (void accept(T t)). It is meant for side effects such as printing or saving. forEach() takes a Consumer. Consumers can be chained with
andThen().
Q20. Explain Supplier with an example.
Supplier<T> takes no arguments and returns a value (T get()). It is used for lazy creation of values, factories, and default values such as Optional.orElseGet() and Stream.generate().

There is no BiSupplier, because a supplier takes no input. If you need more than two arguments, define your own functional interface.
Q22. What are UnaryOperator and BinaryOperator?
They are special cases of Function where the input and output types are the same.
• UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T> - for example String::toUpperCase. Used by
List.replaceAll().
• BinaryOperator<T> extends BiFunction<T,T,T> - for example Integer::sum. Used by reduce(). It also provides BinaryOperator.minBy(comparator) and maxBy(comparator).
Q23. Why do primitive functional interfaces like IntPredicate and IntFunction exist?
Generics only work with objects, so Predicate<Integer> must box each int into an Integer. Boxing and unboxing cost memory and CPU time, especially in large streams. Primitive versions avoid it:
• IntPredicate, LongPredicate, DoublePredicate
• IntFunction<R>, ToIntFunction<T>, IntToLongFunction
• IntUnaryOperator, IntBinaryOperator
• IntConsumer, IntSupplier, BooleanSupplier

IntPredicate positive = i -> i > 0;          // no boxing
ToIntFunction<String> len = String::length;
Q24. What is the difference between andThen() and compose() in Function?
Both chain two functions, but in opposite orders.
• f.andThen(g) runs f first, then g: g(f(x)).
• f.compose(g) runs g first, then f: f(g(x)).
Q25. How do you combine predicates?
Predicate has the default methods and(), or() and negate(), plus the static method
Predicate.isEqual(). (Predicate.not() was added later, in Java 11.)
Q26. What is Function.identity()?
Function.identity() returns a function that always returns its input unchanged (t -> t). It is mostly used as a key or value mapper in collectors.
Q27. How do you create a custom functional interface?
Declare an interface with one abstract method, and preferably annotate it with @FunctionalInterface. This is useful when you need three or more parameters or need to throw checked exceptions.
Questions 28 - 33
Q28. What is a method reference?
A method reference is a shorthand for a lambda that does nothing except call an existing method. It uses the :: operator. It makes code more readable when the lambda just forwards its arguments.
Q29. What are the four types of method references?
• Static method: ClassName::staticMethod - for example Integer::parseInt, which means s ->
Integer.parseInt(s).
• Instance method of a particular object: object::method - for example System.out::println, which means x -> System.out.println(x).
• Instance method of an arbitrary object of a type: ClassName::instanceMethod - for example
String::toUpperCase, which means s -> s.toUpperCase().
• Constructor: ClassName::new - for example ArrayList::new, which means () -> new ArrayList<>().

Q31. What is the difference between object::method and ClassName::instanceMethod?
With object::method the receiver is a specific, already-existing object. Every call goes to that same object, and the lambda arguments become method arguments.
With ClassName::instanceMethod the receiver is the first argument of the lambda. The remaining arguments (if any) are passed to the method.
Q32. What is a constructor reference?
A constructor reference, ClassName::new, creates objects. The compiler chooses the matching constructor from the functional interface's parameters. Array constructors are also supported with
int[]::new.

Supplier<List<String>> s = ArrayList::new;            // new ArrayList<>()
Function<String, StringBuilder> f = StringBuilder::new; // new StringBuilder(str)
BiFunction<String, Integer, Employee> e = Employee::new; // new Employee(name, age)
 
String[] arr = Stream.of("a", "b").toArray(String[]::new);
Q33. When should you use a method reference instead of a lambda?

Use a method reference when the lambda only calls one existing method with the same arguments in the same order - it is shorter and easier to read. Use a lambda when you need extra logic, different argument order, constants, or more than one statement. For example, x -> x + 1 or s ->
s.substring(1) cannot be written as method references.
Questions 34 - 40
Q34. What is a default method?
A default method is an interface method with a body, marked with the default keyword. Implementing classes inherit it automatically and may override it.
Q35. Why were default methods added to Java 8?

To allow interface evolution without breaking existing code. The JDK team needed to add methods such as forEach(), stream(), removeIf() and spliterator() to Collection and Iterable. Without default methods, every class in the world that implements List would have stopped compiling. Default methods supply a standard implementation that old classes inherit automatically.
Q36. How does Java resolve the "diamond problem" with default methods?
When a class inherits the same default method from two interfaces, Java applies three rules:
• Classes win: a method declared in the class or a superclass takes priority over any interface default.
• More specific interfaces win: if interface B extends A, B's default is chosen over A's.
• Otherwise the class must override the method explicitly, or compilation fails. Inside the override it can pick one using InterfaceName.super.method().
Q37. What are static methods in interfaces?

Java 8 lets interfaces define static methods with a body. They belong to the interface itself, are called with InterfaceName.method(), and are not inherited by implementing classes. They are good for utility and factory methods that belong with the interface, for example Comparator.comparing(),
Function.identity() and Stream.of().
Q38. Can a default method override equals(), hashCode() or toString()?

No. Declaring a default method that matches a public method of java.lang.Object is a compile-time error. Because the "classes win" rule means the Object version would always be used anyway, such a default could never be called and would only mislead readers.
Q39. What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class after Java 8?
Default methods narrowed the gap, but important differences remain:
• State: An abstract class can have instance fields and constructors. An interface can only have
public static final constants.
• Inheritance: A class can extend only one abstract class, but can implement many interfaces.
• Access modifiers: Abstract class methods can be protected or private. Java 8 interface methods are always public (private interface methods came in Java 9).
• Purpose: Use an abstract class for a shared base with common state. Use an interface to define a capability or contract.
Q40. How do you call an interface's default method from an overriding method?
Use the syntax InterfaceName.super.methodName(). This works only for interfaces that the class implements directly.
Questions 41 - 75
Q41. What is a Stream in Java 8?

A Stream (java.util.stream.Stream) is a sequence of elements that supports aggregate operations, processed in a pipeline. It does not store data; it takes elements from a source (collection, array, file, generator), passes them through intermediate operations, and produces a result through a terminal operation.

List<String> result = names.stream()        // source
        .filter(n -> n.startsWith("A"))     // intermediate
        .map(String::toUpperCase)           // intermediate
        .sorted()                           // intermediate
        .collect(Collectors.toList());      // terminal
Q42. What is the difference between a Collection and a Stream?
• Storage: A collection stores its elements in memory. A stream stores nothing; it computes elements on demand.
• Evaluation: A collection is eagerly built. A stream is lazily evaluated.
• Iteration: Collections use external iteration (you write the loop). Streams use internal iteration (the library runs the loop).
• Reuse: A collection can be iterated many times. A stream can be consumed only once.
• Modification: You can add and remove items in a collection. A stream never modifies its source.
• Size: A collection is finite. A stream can be infinite (Stream.iterate, Stream.generate).

Q44. What are intermediate and terminal operations?
Intermediate operations return a new stream and are lazy - nothing happens until a terminal operation is called. Examples: filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted, peek, limit, skip.
Terminal operations start processing, produce a result or side effect, and close the stream. Examples: forEach, collect, reduce, count, min, max, anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch, findFirst, findAny,
toArray.
Q45. What is lazy evaluation in streams?

Intermediate operations only describe the work. Elements are pulled through the pipeline one at a time only when a terminal operation asks for them. This lets streams skip unneeded work, combine operations into one pass, and handle infinite streams.
Q46. How does filter() work?
filter(Predicate<T>) keeps only the elements for which the predicate returns true. It is a stateless intermediate operation, and the output stream can be the same size as the input or smaller.

List<Integer> evens = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).stream()
        .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());     // [2, 4, 6]
Q47. How does map() work?
map(Function<T,R>) transforms each element into exactly one new element, possibly of a different type. The output stream always has the same number of elements as the input.

List<Integer> lengths = Arrays.asList("Java", "Stream", "API").stream()
        .map(String::length)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());     // [4, 6, 3]
Primitive versions mapToInt, mapToLong and mapToDouble return primitive streams and avoid boxing.
Q48. What is the difference between map() and flatMap()?
map() is a one-to-one transformation: each element becomes one element. flatMap() is a one-to-many transformation: each element becomes a stream, and all those streams are flattened into one stream.
Q49. Explain distinct(), sorted(), limit() and skip().
• distinct() removes duplicates using equals() and hashCode().
• sorted() sorts by natural order; sorted(Comparator) sorts with a custom order.
• limit(n) keeps at most the first n elements (short-circuiting).
• skip(n) discards the first n elements.

Stream.of(5, 3, 1, 3, 5, 9, 7)
      .distinct()          // 5, 3, 1, 9, 7
      .sorted()            // 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
      .skip(1)             // 3, 5, 7, 9
      .limit(2)            // 3, 5
      .forEach(System.out::println);
skip and limit together are a simple way to paginate: skip(page * size).limit(size).
Q50. What is peek() used for?

peek(Consumer) runs an action on each element as it passes through and returns the same stream unchanged. It is mainly for debugging - seeing values between pipeline stages. Do not rely on it for business logic, because it runs only if a terminal operation pulls elements through it.

List<String> out = Stream.of("one", "two", "three")
        .filter(s -> s.length() > 3)
        .peek(s -> System.out.println("Filtered: " + s))
        .map(String::toUpperCase)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());
Q51. What is the difference between forEach() and forEachOrdered()?

On a sequential stream they behave the same. On a parallel stream, forEach() processes elements in whatever order threads finish them (non-deterministic, faster), while forEachOrdered() guarantees the source's encounter order (deterministic, but loses some of the parallel benefit).

Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).parallelStream().forEach(System.out::print);        // e.g. 34152
Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).parallelStream().forEachOrdered(System.out::print); // 12345
Q52. What is reduce()? Explain its three forms.
reduce() combines all elements of a stream into a single value by applying a function repeatedly.
• reduce(identity, accumulator) returns a T. The identity is the starting value and the result if the stream is empty.
• reduce(accumulator) returns an Optional<T>, because the stream may be empty.
• reduce(identity, accumulator, combiner) is used when the result type differs from the element type, or in parallel streams where the combiner merges partial results.

List<Integer> nums = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
int sum = nums.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum);           // 15
Optional<Integer> max = nums.stream().reduce(Integer::max); // Optional[5]
int product = nums.stream().reduce(1, (a, b) -> a * b);    // 120
 
int totalLen = Stream.of("ab", "cde")
        .reduce(0, (acc, s) -> acc + s.length(), Integer::sum);  // 5
Q53. What is collect() and the Collectors class?

collect() is a terminal operation that performs a mutable reduction: it gathers stream elements into a container such as a List, Set, Map or String. The Collectors class supplies ready-made collectors:
toList, toSet, toMap, toCollection, joining, groupingBy, partitioningBy, counting, summingInt,
averagingDouble, mapping, minBy, maxBy, reducing, collectingAndThen and more.

TreeSet<String> sorted = names.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));
Q54. How do Collectors.toList(), toSet() and toMap() differ?
• toList() collects to a List (an ArrayList in practice) and keeps duplicates and order.
• toSet() collects to a Set (a HashSet in practice), removing duplicates without any order guarantee.
• toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper) builds a Map from each element.

List<String> list = Stream.of("a", "b", "a").collect(Collectors.toList());  // [a, b, a]
Set<String>  set  = Stream.of("a", "b", "a").collect(Collectors.toSet());   // [a, b]
Map<String, Integer> map = Stream.of("apple", "kiwi")
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(s -> s, String::length));   // {apple=5, kiwi=4}
Neither toList() nor toSet() guarantees the exact implementation type. Use
toCollection(LinkedList::new) if you need a specific one.
Q55. What happens with duplicate keys in Collectors.toMap()?
The two-argument toMap throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key. Pass a third argument - a merge function - to decide which value to keep, and an optional fourth argument to choose the Map type.
Also note that toMap throws a NullPointerException if a value is null.
Q56. How does Collectors.groupingBy() work?

groupingBy(classifier) groups elements into a Map<K, List<T>>, where the key is the result of the classifier function. A second argument (a downstream collector) changes what is stored for each group, and a three-argument version also chooses the map type.
Q57. What is partitioningBy() and how is it different from groupingBy()?
partitioningBy(predicate) splits elements into exactly two groups and returns a Map<Boolean,
List<T>> with keys true and false. Both keys are always present, even when a group is empty.
groupingBy can create any number of groups, and only creates keys that actually appear.
Q58. How does Collectors.joining() work?
joining() concatenates CharSequence elements into one String. It has three forms: no separator, with a delimiter, and with a delimiter, prefix and suffix.

List<String> langs = Arrays.asList("Java", "Kotlin", "Scala");
langs.stream().collect(Collectors.joining());               // JavaKotlinScala
langs.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(", "));           // Java, Kotlin, Scala
langs.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]")); // [Java, Kotlin, Scala]
Q59. What are counting(), summingInt(), averagingInt() and summarizingInt()?
These are numeric collectors, often used as downstream collectors inside groupingBy.
• counting() returns the number of elements as a Long.
• summingInt/Long/Double(mapper) returns the sum.
• averagingInt/Long/Double(mapper) returns the average as a Double.
• summarizingInt/Long/Double(mapper) returns an IntSummaryStatistics object with count, sum, min, average and max in one pass.

IntSummaryStatistics stats = Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc")
        .collect(Collectors.summarizingInt(String::length));
stats.getMax();       // 3
stats.getAverage();   // 2.0
stats.getSum();       // 6
Q60. What are downstream collectors like mapping()?
A downstream collector is a collector passed into another collector (usually groupingBy or
partitioningBy) to process the elements of each group. mapping(mapper, downstream) transforms each element before collecting it.
Q61. Explain anyMatch(), allMatch() and noneMatch().
They are short-circuiting terminal operations that return a boolean.
• anyMatch(p) is true if at least one element matches. It stops at the first match.
• allMatch(p) is true if every element matches. It stops at the first failure.
• noneMatch(p) is true if no element matches.
For an empty stream: anyMatch returns false, while allMatch and noneMatch return true.

List<Integer> n = Arrays.asList(2, 4, 6, 7);
n.stream().anyMatch(x -> x > 6);        // true
n.stream().allMatch(x -> x % 2 == 0);   // false
n.stream().noneMatch(x -> x < 0);       // true
Q62. What is the difference between findFirst() and findAny()?

Both return an Optional<T> and short-circuit. findFirst() always returns the first element in encounter order. findAny() may return any element; on sequential streams it usually returns the first, but on parallel streams it returns whichever is found fastest, which performs better when order does not matter.

Optional<String> first = Stream.of("a", "b", "c").findFirst();          // a
Optional<String> any   = Stream.of("a", "b", "c").parallel().findAny(); // any of them
Q63. How do you find the min and max of a stream?
min(Comparator) and max(Comparator) return an Optional<T>. Primitive streams have min() and max() with no arguments that return OptionalInt, OptionalDouble and so on.

List<Integer> nums = Arrays.asList(4, 9, 1, 7);
nums.stream().max(Integer::compare).get();            // 9
nums.stream().min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).get();   // 1
nums.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).max().getAsInt();  // 9
 
Optional<String> longest = Stream.of("hi", "hello", "hey")
        .max(Comparator.comparing(String::length));   // hello
Q64. What are short-circuiting operations?
These operations can finish without processing every element. This is what makes infinite streams usable.
• Intermediate: limit().
• Terminal: findFirst(), findAny(), anyMatch(), allMatch(), noneMatch().

Stream.iterate(1, n -> n + 1)       // infinite
      .filter(n -> n % 7 == 0)
      .limit(3)                     // short-circuits
      .forEach(System.out::println);  // 7 14 21
Q65. Can a stream be reused after a terminal operation?
No. A stream can be traversed only once. After a terminal operation has run, any further call throws
IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. If you need to run the pipeline again, create a new stream, or use a Supplier<Stream<T>>.
Q66. What are primitive streams? Explain boxed() and mapToObj().
IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream hold primitives directly, avoiding boxing. They add numeric methods such as sum(), average(), range() and summaryStatistics().
• mapToInt() and similar convert an object stream to a primitive stream.
• boxed() converts a primitive stream into a Stream<Integer> (or Long or Double).
• mapToObj() converts each primitive into an object.

int total = Stream.of("a", "bb").mapToInt(String::length).sum();    // 3
List<Integer> list = IntStream.of(3, 1, 2).boxed().collect(Collectors.toList());
List<String> labels = IntStream.range(1, 4)
        .mapToObj(i -> "Item" + i).collect(Collectors.toList());   // [Item1, Item2, Item3]
OptionalDouble avg = IntStream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).average();           // 2.5
Q67. What is the difference between IntStream.range() and rangeClosed()?
range(start, end) excludes the end value. rangeClosed(start, end) includes it.

IntStream.range(1, 5).forEach(System.out::print);        // 1234
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).forEach(System.out::print);  // 12345
Q68. How do Stream.iterate() and Stream.generate() create infinite streams?
• Stream.iterate(seed, UnaryOperator) produces seed, f(seed), f(f(seed)), and so on - each value is computed from the previous one.
• Stream.generate(Supplier) calls the supplier each time to produce independent values.
Both are infinite, so you must stop them with limit() or a short-circuiting terminal operation. (Java 9 added iterate(seed, hasNext, next) with a condition.)

Stream.iterate(1, x -> x * 3).limit(5).forEach(System.out::println);  // 1 3 9 27 81
Stream.generate(() -> "Hi").limit(3).forEach(System.out::println);    // Hi Hi Hi
Q69. What are parallel streams?
A parallel stream splits its source into chunks and processes them on several threads of the common
ForkJoinPool, then combines the results. You create one with collection.parallelStream() or
stream.parallel(). The pool size defaults to the number of CPU cores minus one.

long count = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10_000_000)
        .parallel()
        .filter(n -> n % 3 == 0)
        .count();
Q70. When should you avoid parallel streams?
• Small datasets: splitting and merging cost more than the work saved.
• Shared mutable state: for example, adding to an ArrayList from forEach causes race conditions.
• Order-dependent operations: limit, findFirst and forEachOrdered are expensive in parallel.
• Blocking I/O: database or network calls block the shared common pool and slow down every parallel stream in the application.
• Sources that split poorly: LinkedList, Stream.iterate and I/O streams. ArrayList, arrays and
IntStream.range split well.
Always measure before and after - parallel is not automatically faster.
Q71. What are stateless and stateful intermediate operations?
Stateless operations (filter, map, flatMap, peek) process each element independently and need no memory of other elements.

Stateful operations (distinct, sorted, limit, skip) need information about other elements. sorted() must see all elements before it can output the first one. Stateful operations are more expensive, especially in parallel streams, and sorted() cannot work on an infinite stream.
Q72. In what order are stream operations executed?

Streams process elements vertically, one element at a time through the whole pipeline, rather than running each operation over the whole collection in turn. Stateful operations such as sorted() are the exception: they act as a barrier. Because of this, putting filter before map reduces the work done.
Q73. What is Collectors.collectingAndThen()?
It applies a finishing function to the result of another collector. Common uses are making the result unmodifiable, or unwrapping the Optional returned by maxBy or minBy.

List<String> unmodifiable = Stream.of("a", "b")
        .collect(Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(),
                 Collections::unmodifiableList));
 
Map<String, Employee> topByDept = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDept,
                 Collectors.collectingAndThen(
                     Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary)),
                     Optional::get)));
Q74. How do you sort a Map by its values using streams?
Stream the map's entrySet(), sort it with Map.Entry.comparingByValue(), and collect into a
LinkedHashMap to keep the sorted order.
Q75. What is the difference between Arrays.stream() and Stream.of()?
For object arrays they behave the same. The difference shows with primitive arrays:
Arrays.stream(int[]) returns an IntStream of the numbers, while Stream.of(int[]) returns a
Stream<int[]> containing a single element - the whole array. Arrays.stream() also accepts a start and end index.

int[] arr = {1, 2, 3};
Arrays.stream(arr).sum();          // 6 - IntStream
Stream.of(arr).count();            // 1 - Stream<int[]> with one element
Arrays.stream(arr, 1, 3).sum();    // 5 - elements at index 1 and 2
Questions 76 - 83
Q76. What is Optional and why was it introduced?

Optional<T> is a container that holds either one non-null value or nothing. It makes "this value may be missing" explicit in a method's return type, forces callers to think about the empty case, and reduces
NullPointerExceptions. It also offers a fluent API (map, filter, orElse) instead of nested null checks.

Optional<String> name = findUserName(42);
String display = name.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("GUEST");
Q77. How do you create an Optional?
• Optional.of(value) - the value must be non-null, otherwise it throws NullPointerException.
• Optional.ofNullable(value) - returns an empty Optional if the value is null.
• Optional.empty() - an empty Optional.
Q78. What is the difference between isPresent() and ifPresent()?
isPresent() returns a boolean telling you whether a value exists - it leads to imperative if checks.
ifPresent(Consumer) runs the given action only if a value exists, which is the cleaner, functional style. (Java 11 added isEmpty(), and Java 9 added ifPresentOrElse().)
Q79. What is the difference between orElse() and orElseGet()?
orElse(value) always evaluates its argument, even when the Optional has a value.
orElseGet(Supplier) only calls the supplier when the Optional is empty. If the default is expensive to compute (a database call or object creation), use orElseGet.
Q80. How does orElseThrow() work?

orElseThrow(Supplier<? extends X>) returns the value if present; otherwise it throws the exception created by the supplier. It is the standard way to handle "must exist" lookups. (Java 10 added a no-argument version that throws NoSuchElementException.)

User user = userRepo.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException("No user: " + id));
Q81. How do map(), flatMap() and filter() work on Optional?
• map(f) applies f to the value if present and wraps the result in an Optional.
• flatMap(f) is used when f itself returns an Optional, so you avoid Optional<Optional<T>>.
• filter(p) keeps the value only if it satisfies the predicate; otherwise the result is empty.
Q82. What are the best practices for using Optional?
Do:
• Use Optional as a method return type when a result may be absent.
• Prefer orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, map and ifPresent over get().
• Return Optional.empty() - never return null from a method that returns Optional.
Avoid:
• Optional as a field, method parameter, or in collections - it is not Serializable and adds overhead.
• Optional<List<T>> - return an empty list instead.
• Using isPresent() followed by get() - that is just a null check written differently.
Q83. Why is Optional.get() considered risky?

get() throws NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty, so calling it without checking simply replaces a NullPointerException with another runtime exception. Use the safer alternatives: orElse(),
orElseGet(), orElseThrow() or ifPresent(). (Java 10 added orElseThrow() with no arguments as a clearer-named equivalent of get().)
Questions 84 - 92
Q84. Why was a new Date/Time API introduced in Java 8?
The old java.util.Date and Calendar classes had serious problems:
• Mutable and not thread-safe - SimpleDateFormat in particular breaks when shared between threads.
• Poor design - months start at 0, years are offset from 1900, and Date actually represents an instant, not a date.
• Weak time-zone support and no separate types for a date-only or time-only value.
The new java.time package, based on the Joda-Time library (JSR-310), is immutable, thread-safe, clearly designed and follows ISO-8601.
Q85. What are LocalDate, LocalTime and LocalDateTime?
They represent date and time values without a time zone.
• LocalDate - a date only, such as 2026-11-18 (birthdays, holidays).
• LocalTime - a time only, such as 10:30:15 (opening hours).
• LocalDateTime - both date and time, such as 2026-11-18T10:30.
Q86. What are ZonedDateTime and ZoneId?

ZoneId identifies a time zone, such as Asia/Kolkata or America/New_York. ZonedDateTime is a date-time together with a time zone, and it handles daylight-saving rules correctly. OffsetDateTime stores a fixed offset (like +05:30) without zone rules.
Q87. What is Instant?

Instant is a single point on the timeline in UTC, measured in seconds and nanoseconds since the epoch (1970-01-01T00:00:00Z). It is meant for machines: timestamps, logging, measuring durations, and storing event times in databases.
Q88. What is the difference between Period and Duration?
• Period is a date-based amount in years, months and days. Use it with LocalDate - for example, to calculate someone's age.
• Duration is a time-based amount in seconds and nanoseconds. Use it with LocalTime,
LocalDateTime or Instant.
Q89. How do you format and parse dates with DateTimeFormatter?
DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe (unlike SimpleDateFormat), so it can be stored in a static constant. Use predefined formatters like ISO_LOCAL_DATE or a custom pattern with ofPattern().
Q90. Why are java.time classes immutable, and what does that mean in practice?

Every java.time class is immutable: methods like plusDays() or withYear() return a new object and leave the original unchanged. This makes them thread-safe without synchronisation and safe to share or cache. A common mistake is to ignore the return value:

Java 8 added bridge methods: Date.toInstant(), Date.from(Instant) and Calendar.toInstant(). Go through Instant and a ZoneId.
Q92. What are TemporalAdjusters and ChronoUnit?

TemporalAdjusters provides common date adjustments such as first or last day of the month and next Monday. ChronoUnit is an enum of time units and can measure the distance between two dates in a single unit.

Questions 93 - 100
Q93. What are StringJoiner and String.join()?
StringJoiner builds a delimited string with an optional prefix and suffix, and lets you set a value to return when nothing was added. String.join() is a static shortcut for the simple case.
Collectors.joining() uses StringJoiner internally.
Q94. What new methods were added to the Map interface?
• getOrDefault(key, default) - returns the default when the key is missing.
• putIfAbsent(key, value) - puts only if the key is missing.
• computeIfAbsent(key, fn) - computes and stores a value if missing. Ideal for "map of lists".
• computeIfPresent(key, fn) and compute(key, fn) - recompute an existing value.
• merge(key, value, fn) - inserts the value, or combines it with the existing one. Ideal for counters.
• forEach(BiConsumer), replaceAll(BiFunction), remove(key, value), replace(key, old, new).
Q95. What new methods were added to Iterable, Collection and List?
• Iterable.forEach(Consumer) - internal iteration over any collection.
• Collection.removeIf(Predicate) - removes every matching element safely (no
ConcurrentModificationException).
• Collection.stream() and parallelStream().
• List.replaceAll(UnaryOperator) - transforms every element in place.
• List.sort(Comparator) - sorts the list in place.
• Iterator.forEachRemaining(Consumer).

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
nums.removeIf(n -> n % 2 == 0);       // [1, 3, 5]
nums.replaceAll(n -> n * 10);         // [10, 30, 50]
nums.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder()); // [50, 30, 10]
Q96. What is CompletableFuture?

CompletableFuture<T> (in java.util.concurrent) is a Future that can be completed manually and that supports non-blocking, chainable asynchronous code. Unlike the old Future, you do not have to block on get(): you attach callbacks, combine several futures, and handle errors in a pipeline. By default async tasks run on the common ForkJoinPool, or on an Executor you supply.

CompletableFuture<String> cf = CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(1))          // runs asynchronously
        .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)           // transform the result
        .exceptionally(ex -> "DEFAULT");          // recover from errors
 
cf.thenAccept(System.out::println);               // callback when done
String result = cf.join();                        // block only if needed
Other useful methods: runAsync, allOf, anyOf, handle, whenComplete and complete.
Q97. What is the difference between thenApply(), thenCompose() and thenCombine()?
• thenApply(fn) transforms the result synchronously, like map. Use it when fn returns a plain value.
• thenCompose(fn) is used when fn itself returns a CompletableFuture. It flattens the result, like
flatMap, so you avoid CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>.
• thenCombine(other, fn) waits for two independent futures and combines their results.
Q98. What changed in ConcurrentHashMap in Java 8?
• No more segments: Java 7 locked one of 16 segments. Java 8 uses CAS (compare-and-swap) operations plus synchronized on the first node of an individual bucket, so concurrency is much finer-grained.

• Treeification: a bucket with many collisions (8 or more entries, in a table of at least 64) turns its linked list into a red-black tree, so worst-case lookup becomes O(log n) instead of O(n). HashMap got the same improvement.
• New bulk operations: forEach, search, reduce with a parallelism threshold, plus mappingCount() and ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().
• Atomic compute, computeIfAbsent and merge.
Q99. What is Metaspace, and how is it different from PermGen?
Java 8 removed the Permanent Generation (PermGen) and replaced it with Metaspace to store class metadata.
• PermGen was part of the Java heap and had a fixed maximum size (-XX:MaxPermSize), so applications that loaded many classes often failed with OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space.
• Metaspace lives in native memory and grows automatically by default. You can cap it with
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
• Interned strings and static variables moved to the regular heap.
The result is fewer out-of-memory errors related to class loading and less tuning work.
Q100. What other features were introduced in Java 8?
• Base64 - java.util.Base64 with basic, URL-safe and MIME encoders and decoders.
• Nashorn - a faster JavaScript engine replacing Rhino (later removed in Java 15).
• Repeating annotations - @Repeatable lets the same annotation appear more than once on one element.
• Type annotations - annotations can be placed on any use of a type, for example @NonNull String.
• Parallel array sorting - Arrays.parallelSort().
• Arithmetic helpers - Math.addExact() and multiplyExact() throw on overflow.
• Unsigned arithmetic - Integer.toUnsignedString() and Integer.divideUnsigned().
• StampedLock, LongAdder and LongAccumulator for high-performance concurrency.
• jdeps - a tool to analyse class dependencies.

Q1. What is Java and what are its main features?
BEGINNER

Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented language created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (1995), now owned by Oracle. Source code is compiled to bytecode that runs on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), so the same .class file runs on any OS that has a JVM.
• Platform independent – "Write Once, Run Anywhere" (WORA).
• Object-oriented – everything is modelled with classes and objects (primitives are the only exception).
• Robust – strong typing, no pointer arithmetic, automatic garbage collection, checked exceptions.
• Secure – bytecode verifier, no direct memory access, sandboxing.
• Multithreaded – threads and concurrency utilities are built into the language and library.
• High performance – the JIT compiler turns hot bytecode into native machine code.
• Rich standard library – collections, I/O, networking, concurrency and more.

Q4. Explain the JVM architecture.
INTERMEDIATE
The JVM has three main subsystems:

• Class Loader Subsystem – loads .class files, then links them (verify bytecode, prepare static fields with defaults, resolve symbolic references) and initializes them (runs static blocks and static initializers).

• Runtime Data Areas – Method Area/Metaspace (class metadata, static variables), Heap (all objects), JVM Stack (one per thread, holds frames), PC Register (per thread, current instruction), Native Method Stack.
• Execution Engine – the Interpreter executes bytecode line by line; the JIT compiler compiles frequently executed ("hot") methods into native code; the Garbage Collector frees unreachable objects.
JNI (Java Native Interface) lets Java call native C/C++ libraries.

INTERVIEW TIP Heap and Method Area are shared by all threads; Stack, PC register and Native stack are per thread.

java.util.*).
• Platform (called Extension before Java 9) – loads other platform modules.
• Application/System – loads classes from your classpath.

Parent delegation: when asked to load a class, a loader first delegates to its parent. Only if the parent cannot find it does the child try. This prevents someone from replacing core classes (e.g. a fake java.lang.String) and ensures each class is loaded once.

Q105. How does HashMap work internally?
INTERMEDIATE
HashMap stores entries in an array of buckets (Node<K,V>[] table, default size 16).
• put(k, v): compute hashCode(), spread it with h ^ (h >>> 16), find bucket index (n - 1) & hash.
• If the bucket is empty, store a new node. Otherwise walk the bucket: if a key is equals(), replace its value; else append a new node.
• get(k): same hash → index → walk the bucket using equals().
• When a bucket has more than 8 nodes (and the table has at least 64 buckets) the list becomes a Red-Black tree (treeification) so worst-case lookups are O(log n) instead of O(n).
• When size > capacity × loadFactor (0.75), the table doubles and entries are redistributed.

• Load factor – how full the table may get before resizing (default 0.75).

• Rehashing/resizing – when size exceeds threshold, capacity doubles and every entry is moved to its new bucket. Since capacity is a power of two, each entry either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity.

^ (h >>> 16) spreading step mixes high bits into those low bits to reduce collisions.

Q139. What is the difference between notify() and notifyAll()?
INTERMEDIATE

notify() wakes one arbitrary thread waiting on the object's monitor; notifyAll() wakes all of them, and they compete to re-acquire the lock. Prefer notifyAll() unless you are sure all waiters are equivalent – notify() can wake the "wrong" thread and cause a missed signal (liveness bug).
Q140. What is the join() method?
BEGINNER
t.join() makes the current thread wait until thread t finishes. join(ms) waits at most that long.

Q141. What are yield() and thread priority?
BEGINNER

Q142. What is a daemon thread?
BEGINNER
A low-priority background service thread (e.g. the garbage collector). The JVM exits when only daemon threads remain; it does not wait for them to finish. Set with setDaemon(true) before
start(). finally blocks in daemon threads may not run at shutdown.

Q143. What is synchronization? Why is it needed?
BEGINNER

Synchronization controls access to shared mutable state so that only one thread executes a critical section at a time. It provides mutual exclusion (atomicity) and visibility (changes made inside the lock are seen by the next thread acquiring it). Without it, threads interleave and corrupt data – a race condition.

Q144. What is a race condition? Show an example and fix.
INTERMEDIATE
A race condition occurs when the result depends on the unpredictable timing of threads. count++ is three steps – read, add, write – so two threads can both read the same value and one update is lost.

Q145. What is the difference between a synchronized method and a synchronized block?
INTERMEDIATE

• synchronized static method – locks on the Class object.

• synchronized block – locks on any object you choose, and only for the critical lines. Better: smaller critical section, less contention, and you can use a private lock object that outside code can't grab.

Q146. What is an object monitor / intrinsic lock?
INTERMEDIATE

Every Java object has an intrinsic lock (monitor). A thread entering synchronized(obj) must own obj's monitor; others trying to enter are BLOCKED in the entry set. A thread that calls obj.wait() releases the monitor and moves to the wait set until notified, after which it must re-acquire the lock. Intrinsic locks are reentrant: the owning thread can enter other synchronized blocks on the same object.

Q147. What is the volatile keyword?
INTERMEDIATE

volatile guarantees visibility and ordering: a write to a volatile variable is immediately visible to other threads, and reads/writes are not reordered around it (happens-before). It does not guarantee atomicity of compound operations like count++.
Diagram for Q147. What is the volatile keyword?
JAVA
INTERVIEW TIP Use volatile for flags and safe publication (e.g. double-checked locking); use locks or atomics for read-modify-write.
Q148. What is the difference between volatile and synchronized?

Q149. What is the Java Memory Model and happens-before?
ADVANCED

The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines how threads interact through memory and when writes by one thread are guaranteed visible to another. CPUs and compilers may cache and reorder instructions, so without rules threads could see stale or out-of-order values. Happens-before rules give the guarantees:
• unlock of a monitor happens-before every later lock of the same monitor
• a write to a volatile happens-before every later read of it
• Thread.start() happens-before actions in the started thread
• all actions in a thread happen-before another thread returns from join() on it
• the end of a constructor happens-before the finalizer; final fields are safely published after construction
Q150. What is a deadlock? How do you prevent it?
INTERMEDIATE
A deadlock occurs when two or more threads wait forever for locks held by each other. Four conditions (Coffman) must all hold: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
Diagram for Q150. What is a deadlock? How do you prevent it?
JAVA
Prevention:
• Lock ordering – always acquire locks in the same global order.
• tryLock with timeout (ReentrantLock.tryLock(1, SECONDS)) and back off.
• Keep critical sections small; avoid calling unknown code while holding a lock.
• Use higher-level concurrency utilities.
Detection: thread dump (jstack <pid>) shows "Found one Java-level deadlock".
Q151. What are livelock and starvation?
INTERMEDIATE
• Livelock – threads are not blocked but keep reacting to each other and make no progress (two people stepping aside in the same direction repeatedly). Fix with randomized back-off.
• Starvation – a thread never gets CPU or a lock because others are always favoured (e.g. high-priority threads, unfair locks). Fix with fair locks (new ReentrantLock(true)).

INTERMEDIATE

BEGINNER

The Executor framework (java.util.concurrent) separates task submission from thread management. A thread pool keeps a set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue and are reused. Benefits: no cost of creating a thread per task, bounded resource usage, task queuing, scheduling and lifecycle management.

BEGINNER

Q158. What is the difference between shutdown() and shutdownNow()?
INTERMEDIATE
• shutdown() – stops accepting new tasks but lets already submitted tasks finish.
• shutdownNow() – tries to stop running tasks by interrupting them and returns the list of tasks that never started.
• awaitTermination(timeout) – blocks until all tasks finish or the timeout expires.

Q159. What is a Future? What are its limitations?
INTERMEDIATE
Future<V> represents the result of an asynchronous computation: get() (blocking), get(timeout),
isDone(), cancel(). Limitations: get() blocks; you cannot chain further steps, combine multiple futures, or attach callbacks; and exception handling is clumsy. CompletableFuture solves these.
Q160. What is CompletableFuture?
INTERMEDIATE
A Future that can be completed explicitly and composed into non-blocking pipelines with callbacks.

Q161. What is ReentrantLock and how is it different from synchronized?
INTERMEDIATE

Q162. What is ReadWriteLock?
INTERMEDIATE

ReentrantReadWriteLock has a pair of locks: many threads may hold the read lock simultaneously as long as no thread holds the write lock; the write lock is exclusive. Great for read-heavy data such as caches. StampedLock (Java 8) adds an even cheaper optimistic read.

Q163. What are atomic variables and CAS?
INTERMEDIATE

Classes like AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicReference provide lock-free, thread-safe operations using hardware Compare-And-Swap (CAS): "set the value to new only if it is still expected", retrying in a loop if another thread got there first. No blocking, no deadlock. LongAdder scales even better under heavy contention by spreading updates across cells.

INTERVIEW TIP CAS can suffer from the ABA problem; AtomicStampedReference adds a version stamp to detect it.
Q164. What are CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier and Semaphore?
INTERMEDIATE
• CountDownLatch – one or more threads wait until a count reaches zero via countDown(). One-time use. E.g. main waits for 3 services to start.
• CyclicBarrier – a fixed number of threads wait for each other at a barrier point, then all proceed; reusable. E.g. parallel simulation steps.
• Semaphore – maintains N permits to limit how many threads access a resource concurrently (acquire()/release()). E.g. a pool of 10 DB connections.
JAVA
Q165. What is ThreadLocal?
INTERMEDIATE
ThreadLocal<T> gives each thread its own independent copy of a variable. Common uses: per-thread SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe), user/transaction context in web requests.
JAVA

INTERVIEW TIP In thread pools threads are reused, so always call remove() when done, or values leak into the next task (and can cause memory leaks). ScopedValue (final in Java 25) is a safer alternative for passing context.
Q166. What is the Fork/Join framework?
INTERMEDIATE

A framework for divide-and-conquer parallelism. A task splits itself into subtasks (fork()), computes them in parallel, then combines the results (join()). The ForkJoinPool uses work stealing: idle threads steal queued tasks from busy threads' deques. Parallel streams use the common ForkJoinPool.

Q167. How do you stop a thread? What is interrupt()?
INTERMEDIATE

Thread.stop() is deprecated and unsafe (it releases locks abruptly). The correct way is cooperative cancellation: call t.interrupt(), which sets the interrupt flag; blocking methods (sleep, wait, join,
BlockingQueue.take) throw InterruptedException. The task should check
Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() and exit cleanly.
JAVA
INTERVIEW TIP Never swallow InterruptedException silently – either rethrow it or restore the flag.
Q168. What happens when an exception occurs in a thread?
INTERMEDIATE

An uncaught exception terminates only that thread; other threads keep running. The JVM calls the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler (default prints the stack trace). Set one per thread or globally with
Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler. With submit(), the exception is stored in the Future and appears on get().
JAVA
Q169. What are virtual threads (Java 21)?
ADVANCED

Virtual threads (Project Loom) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than the OS. Millions can exist at once because they are mounted onto a small pool of OS carrier threads only while running; when a virtual thread blocks on I/O, it is unmounted and the carrier runs another one. This lets you write simple blocking, thread-per-request code with the scalability of asynchronous code.
JAVA
Tips: don't pool virtual threads; use them for I/O-bound work, not CPU-bound work. Before Java 24, blocking inside synchronized could pin the carrier thread; Java 24 removed most pinning.
Q170. How do you make a class thread-safe? (strategies summary)
ADVANCED
• Immutability – no shared mutable state at all (best).
• Thread confinement – keep data local to one thread (local variables, ThreadLocal).
• Synchronization – synchronized, ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock.
• Atomic variables – AtomicInteger, LongAdder, AtomicReference.
• Concurrent collections – ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, BlockingQueue.
• Safe publication – final fields, volatile, static initializers.
• Higher-level abstractions – executors, CompletableFuture, structured concurrency, instead of raw threads.

Q191. What is garbage collection? How does the JVM decide an object is garbage?
INTERMEDIATE

Garbage collection automatically reclaims heap memory used by objects that are no longer reachable. The GC starts from GC roots – local variables on thread stacks, static fields, active threads, JNI references – and marks every object reachable through references. Anything not marked is garbage, even if objects reference each other in a cycle (unlike reference counting).
JAVA

Person p = new Person();   // reachable from stack
p = null;                  // now unreachable -> eligible for GC
System.gc();               // only a request; the JVM may ignore it
Q192. Explain the generational heap and minor/major GC.
INTERMEDIATE
Most objects die young (the weak generational hypothesis), so the heap is split:
• Young Generation – Eden + two Survivor spaces (S0, S1). New objects go to Eden. A minor GC copies live objects to a survivor space and clears Eden; it's fast because most objects are dead.
• Old (Tenured) Generation – objects that survive several minor GCs (age threshold, up to 15) are promoted here. Collected by major/full GC, which is slower.
• Metaspace (Java 8+, native memory) – class metadata, replacing PermGen.

Q194. Can there be memory leaks in Java? Give examples.
INTERMEDIATE
Yes. A leak occurs when objects are no longer needed but are still reachable, so the GC cannot reclaim them. Common causes:
• static collections that keep growing (caches without eviction)
• listeners/callbacks registered and never removed
• ThreadLocal values not removed in thread pools
• unclosed resources (streams, connections)
• mutable keys in HashMap whose hash changed
• inner class instances holding an implicit reference to a large outer object

Diagnose with heap dumps (jmap, -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError) and tools like Eclipse MAT, VisualVM or JDK Flight Recorder.

Q196. What are generics and type erasure?
INTERMEDIATE

Generics let classes and methods work with types as parameters, giving compile-time type safety and removing casts. Type erasure: the compiler checks types, then removes generic information, replacing type parameters with their bound (Object by default) and inserting casts. So at runtime
List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class.
JAVA
Consequences: you cannot do new T(), T[] creation, instanceof List<String>, or overload methods that differ only by type parameter.
Q197. What are wildcards? Explain the PECS rule.
INTERMEDIATE
• <?> – unknown type.
• <? extends T> – T or a subtype; you can read T out but cannot add (except null). Producer.
• <? super T> – T or a supertype; you can add T but reads give Object. Consumer.
PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
JAVA
Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) is the classic example.
Q198. What is serialization? What do transient and serialVersionUID do?
INTERMEDIATE
Serialization converts an object into a byte stream (to save to a file or send over a network); deserialization rebuilds it. A class must implement Serializable (a marker interface).
• transient fields are skipped (e.g. passwords, caches); they get default values after deserialization. Static fields are not serialized either.
• serialVersionUID is a version id. If the class changes and the stored id doesn't match, deserialization throws InvalidClassException. Always declare it explicitly.

INTERVIEW TIP Java serialization has a history of security issues; modern apps often prefer JSON (Jackson), Protobuf or records with explicit formats. Never deserialize untrusted data.
Q199. What is reflection? What are its uses and drawbacks?
ADVANCED

Reflection (java.lang.reflect) lets code inspect and manipulate classes, methods, fields and constructors at runtime, even private ones. Frameworks rely on it: Spring (dependency injection), Hibernate (entity mapping), JUnit (finding @Test methods), Jackson (serialization).

Drawbacks: slower than direct calls, breaks encapsulation, loses compile-time checks, and is restricted by the module system (strong encapsulation since Java 16/17).

@FunctionalInterface and @SuppressWarnings. A custom annotation is declared with @interface; meta-annotations control it: @Retention (SOURCE, CLASS, RUNTIME) and @Target (TYPE, METHOD, FIELD …).
